name: Attendance and Early Warning
title: Attendance and Early Warning
answer: Chronic absence is one of the clearest warning signs that a student is struggling, and the strongest response pairs data with a person. A flag from an attendance or early warning system is a reason for a conversation, not a judgment about who a student is.

sections.body: Chronic absence signals that a student is struggling, and messaging parents about absences is only part of the answer. The strongest approach pairs data with a person: a student information system flags rising absences, and an attendance worker, counselor, or teacher follows up by call, meeting, or visit. That person may learn the student is caring for a sick parent, being bullied, or missing the bus. Early warning systems predict risk of failing or dropping out, and machine learning can improve the predictions, but using them well takes expertise. The idea solves the problem of flags that go nowhere or turn into labels, by making every flag the start of human follow up.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the student information system flags students whose absences are rising, and a staff member follows up with a call home, a meeting, or a visit. The same pattern applies to early warning flags for students at risk of failing or dropping out. The text does not give separate grade band guidance, so the practice is described for schools generally rather than by year group. Staff should be trained to treat a flag as a reason for a conversation rather than a judgment about who a student is. Students and families should never be told that a computer has decided a child is at risk.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book reports that messages to parents about their child's absences reduce chronic absence, with effects of 10 to 15 percent in the original trials and smaller effects in newer ones run at scale (Rogers & Feller, 2018; Robinson et al., 2018; Berger et al., 2025). A meta analysis of 13 recent studies of attendance interventions found a small average effect, stronger when carried out within a single school (Li, 2026). On early warning systems, machine learning can improve predictions but takes expertise to use well, and results from systems whose reasoning is hidden can be read through staff members' existing biases (Soland et al., 2020). Predictions are also wrong in ways that matter: interviews with students whose risk predictions were wrong found the errors came from sudden life events such as family changes, health problems, or computer trouble (Hlosta et al., 2022).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Early warning flags should never follow a student as labels. A flag is a reason for a conversation, not a judgment about who a student is, and staff should be trained to see flags this way. Students and families should never be told that a computer has decided a child is at risk. The decisions about what a flag means and what to do next stay with the people who know the student, because the person doing the follow up is the one who learns what is actually happening. Messaging helps, but it is only part of the answer, and predictions can be wrong in ways that matter.
